post.author: AmirMušić
post.text: For 10+ years, I've been creating branding & ads for Warner Music, PepsiCo, and others. Now I combine that experience with AI to build hi-end visual systems faster. This article shows my complete branding workflow with AI This time, I turned one reference into an identity, brand guidelines, packaging, key visuals, and a scalable campaign world. At the end, I’m also sharing the open-source Lovart Brand System Skill - a copy-paste workflow that guides Lovart Agent through the same process. This article is sponsored by @lovart_ai. Thanks to the team for supporting this post and my work for you. ONE REFERENCE -> BRAND SYSTEM I wanted to test one question: Can an AI agent understand why an image works -> not copy it -> and turn that logic into a new brand? So I found a Pinterest image I like, sent it to the Lovart Agent and gave it a minimal brief of the brand I want to build: Brand: Juicee Product: natural, caffeine-free energy drink Audience: active people aged 20–35 Flavors: watermelon, melon, apricot, raspberry From that, we built a visual identity, a complete multi-slide brand system, four connected SKUs, campaign scenes, packaging concepts, videos & more. Lovart accelerated the design process - and my role was to judge & direct the outputs, remove conflicting directions, define the rules & system. My workflow: Reference → Deconstruction → Anchor (Brand Kit) → Guidelines → Brand Lock → Campaign Assets → Packaging Turn one reference into a brand system with Lovart Agent: → amirmushich.link/design_agent 1. DECODE THE REFERENCE I found the reference of the Pickle Potion drink - and this visual gave us four transferable rules: Split-screen composition Real ingredient photography Bold typography Simple starburst elements and more (see below). Pickle Potion uses those rules to communicate briny shock. For my brand - Juicee - I translated them into a different idea: The intensity of freshness - real fruit that hits. The instruction I used Important: A reference should inform the logic - not the design output. 2. FROM DRAFT TO BRAND ANCHOR The first Brand Kit looked okay - but mixed too many styles, patterns, effects, and typography directions. It was content, not a system. My feedback was simple: “Use more white space, less graphic devices, and one clear direction.” My first job was not to generate more. It was to remove. The problem was a lack of hierarchy: Realistic liquid materials, cartoon mascots, icons, product graphics, and several micro-directions were all competing inside one board. Different materials did not match the graphic language, so the brand felt assembled from fragments instead of directed as one world. I rejected it - because it was creatively inconsistent. Correct the direction (if needed): The second version became a great anchor for the future brand - one approved image the entire brand could obey. Here's how the whole process looks like: On this stage, we locked: logo concept; color palette; typography (free Google Fonts); brand graphics (vector starbursts); can design; media rule - "real fruit photography"; design foundation. The system is now locked - let's scale it. 3. TURN THE ANCHOR INTO A BRAND SYSTEM From one anchor, Lovart Agent created a connected set of brand-guideline modules: Logo usage · Typography · Color · Graphic elements · Key visual rules · Packaging · Brand usage rules · Design rules · Photo guidelines The same rules then produced 4 flavor key visuals with one repeatable mechanism: [fruit on the left] → [product on the right] → [one headline] → [one starburst claim] → [one consistent hierarchy] The SKUs feel different without becoming four different brands. 4. EXPAND THE CAMPAIGN (and keep the brand consistent) Once the design system was locked, I introduced 9 additional scene references - to expand the brand campaigns world. Lovart Agent quickly translated those references into a broad range of explorations - from fruit top views and product close-ups to lifestyle scenes. Because each reference carried its own strong visual language, some early outputs began to over-weight its fonts, colors, patterns, and packaging cues alongside the composition. This wasn’t a lack of generation capability - it was a creative-direction challenge. The Agent needed a clearer hierarchy for deciding which source controlled each part of the output. One of Lovart’s strengths is that you can combine references and steer the system iteratively. I used that flexibility to define a clearer reference hierarchy - a workflow I call Brand Lock. Brand Lock isn’t a button or a single prompt. It’s a methodology for deciding what each reference is/isn’t allowed to control. The final scene must still be materially original - not a recreated artwork with a different product. Brand Locking with Lovart Agent combine the scene references, Brand Kit, and packaging board → generate new branded scenes → identify and correct visual drift → reveal the complete scaled canvas The references could now influence the scene language without owning the scene or redesigning the brand. By repeating the same Agent workflow across different references and flavors, I expanded one approved system into dozens of connected visuals. Agent generated the assets Brand Lock kept the system consistent. Precision editing after generation The editing tools came after generation. Text Edit, Touch Edit, and Edit Elements were useful for precise corrections to assets. Refine one completed asset with Text Edit → Touch Edit → Edit Elements The same connected system also produced front, three-quarter, isometric, and exploded packaging views. Note: These are conceptual packaging visualizations - not final dielines, vector artwork, prepress files, production-ready 3D models, or manufacturing specifications. 5. TURN THE BRAND SYSTEM INTO MOTION WITH SEEDANCE 2.5 Once the visual system was locked, I used Seedance 2.5 inside Lovart to generate the motion assets, then assembled and finished the final Juicee ad in Adobe. The same approved packaging, colors, typography, and campaign language became the source of truth for video - so motion extended the system. The Agent kept the creative workflow connected - from static brand assets to video generation on the same Canvas. The brand/character consistency is really strong here. ONE REFERENCE TO A COMPLETE BRAND WORLD The clearest proof of the workflow is my Lovart canvas. Reference → Brand System → Entire brand world. Build a consistent brand system with Lovart Agent → amirmushich.link/design_agent MY BRANDING SKILL (GitHub) I packaged the complete workflow as a copy-paste Skill for Lovart Agent Instead of running prompts manually, paste the Skill into a new Lovart project and let the Agent guide you through: mass-user-friendly onboarding; reference deconstruction; Anchor Brand Kit development; creative-direction critique; fonts selection; generation approval gates; brand guidelines; Brand Lock; campaign assets; consistency audits; packaging concepts. If you don’t know how to answer his questions - or why a visual direction isn’t working - the Skill can help diagnose the problem before you spend more credits. Get the Brand System Skill on GitHub https://amirmushich.link/brand_skill 5 THINGS TO REMEMBER One solid anchor beats twenty disconnected outputs Use references for principles (not for copy-paste) Approve the concept before spending credits on assets Use the Agent to generate complete assets - and editing tools to refine the details AI accelerates concepting; final production still needs human vision THE REAL LESSON We started with one Pinterest image. Working with Lovart, I turned it into an identity, SKUs, brand guidelines, campaign scenes, packaging concepts, and a complete brand world. The agent accelerated exploration and execution. My job was to choose the direction, reject visual contradictions, and define what could change - and what had to stay locked. AI can create endless images. A brand begins when someone decides what must stay in its visual language. Turn your next reference into a brand system with Lovart Agent → amirmushich.link/design_agent One reference can become more than an image. It can become an entire brand world. #BuiltWithLovart #AiDesign #AIBranding

title: Context engineering used to focus on adding information that base models…
note: @posthog: Context engineering used to focus on adding information that base models lacked: But then the models kept getting better. Now, the same context your agents couldn’t function without can make them perform worse. Our AI onboarding wizard, for example, often landed on the wrong…

post.author: PostHog
post.text: Context engineering used to focus on adding information that base models lacked: But then the models kept getting better. Now, the same context your agents couldn’t function without can make them perform worse. Our AI onboarding wizard, for example, often landed on the wrong project in monorepos because our scripts pointed to root by default. Now that models are good at inferring repo structure, we updated it so headless runs take advantage of model recommendations. This is the same reason why Anthropic removed 80% of Claude Code’s system prompt. Labs are going back on previous advice about rules and repetition; judgment, interfaces, and progressive disclosure are the new best practices instead. The goal of context engineering has since shifted toward subtracting as much information as you can to get out of the models’ way: But figuring out exactly what to subtract isn’t easy when dealing with unpredictable behavior. When asked about his approach, Boris Cherny, the creator of Claude Code, recommended deleting your CLAUDE.md every six months to stay on the bleeding edge. Theo recently reported it was worth rewriting his AGENTS.md by hand: If you'd rather not start from scratch every time, here are three practical ways to maintain your context while "unhobbling" AI, from most hands-on to most autonomous. 1. Run /doctor, but follow up with real eyes The simplest way to keep your context healthy is to read and edit it yourself. Most coding agents have a built-in /doctor command to help with this. Anthropic’s version of it runs basic health checks, deletes redundant prompts, catches broken settings, finds unused plugins, and optimizes for lazy loading. The report also prints a summary of how often you’ve used each file, and how much it can trim. Here’s what that looks like for our website’s main AGENTS.md: Across the posthog.com repo, it suggested turning off 3 unused plugins and 3 skills across our website repo and estimated saving an average of 6K tokens per session. This is decent, but you can’t rely on it to catch everything because it doesn’t check for correctness; it acts only based on what it can derive from your code. For example, last month, we started using merge queues and added this line to our AGENTS.md: “All merges into master go through the Trunk merge queue. Never run gh pr merge.” A couple days later, we paused the queue to fix some failing tests and forgot to update that line. Our agents therefore had wrong instructions for 21 hours. During that time, one engineer’s PR got stuck for 10 hours; another lost 45 minutes investigating the cause before updating the instructions. We didn’t use claude doctor in the posthog monorepo to fix this, but it couldn’t have caught it anyway since merge queue state lives in a GitHub setting rather than in code. Agents don’t know what they don’t know. Try this: Run claude doctor after each upgrade and follow up with a manual pass on your AGENTS.md. For each line, if you can’t name the failure it prevents, delete it. 2. Test your context like it’s code Another tool for maintaining and unhobbling your context is evals. It’s just like adding regression tests whenever you fix a bug in code. Every time you update your context to address an agent’s mistake, capture what caused it in the first place as an eval. For example, we record technical “gotchas” we see from real PostHog Wizard runs as framework-specific commandments such as: For versions 15.3+, initialize PostHog in instrumentation-client.ts for the simplest setup. For Phoenix or Plug apps, add PostHog.Integrations.Plug before the router so request context is attached to captured events and errors posthog-rs is the Rust SDK crate; add it with cargo add posthog-rs and construct the client with posthog_rs::client(options).await. These get combined with instructions from the context-mill (e.g., “reuse event names the project already uses”) and a set of ~40 clean sample apps to create the evals we use in the wizard-ci. Here’s how it works: wizard-ci runs the PostHog Wizard on all ~40 sample apps and creates one PR for each. Those PRs don’t get merged. Instead, a second agent called the pr-evaluator grades each of them based on the diffs and session logs. The pr-evaluator leaves metrics and reports on the trigger PR and the wizard-ci PR. These reports help us catch issues like the wizard skipping installing PostHog entirely because the model determined it was already complete: wizard-ci is just one of many context-as-code tools we’ve built in our wizard-workbench. The setup is complex since it maintains our biggest conversion path, but the core concept is easy to apply: test your context by saving prompts that check if your agents are doing what you want them to do. Try this: The next time your agent makes a mistake, paste the prompt that caused it into a failures.md. Re-run those prompts the next time you edit or delete parts of your AGENTS.md as a quick test suite for your highest-cost piece of context. 3. Ask agents for feedback directly Another option for fixing your context is to just ask. Agents are good at providing feedback about how they would improve your context while they’re using it. Many developers already do this to update their skills, but you can take it further by putting it in your prompts by default. For example, the final instruction for the PostHog Wizard says to send back a quick remark about any errors they encountered in production: “What information or guidance would have been useful to have in the integration prompt or documentation for this task? Specifically anything that would have prevented tool failures, erroneous edits, or other wasted turns.” This gives us a rich feed of live bug reports for cheap – a basic form of AI observability: We took this even further by feeding them back into our context-mill with a loop, making it self-driving. But since we can't trust agents at face value, we cluster and verify the underlying issues first. Here's what the feedback clusters looked like for the last month: Half of the other category is just confirmation messages like “succeeded on the first attempt,” or “posthog-js already installed”. The other half is a long tail of issues that weren’t common enough to cluster. Once the loop identifies a meaningful cluster, it deploys subagents to verify the issue before attempting a fix. For example, to check the notebook create schema/tool issue, a subagent followed the legacy instructions to reproduce the hand-splicing text failure that was addressed in this PR. This approach works best at scale to cluster remarks, but you can still apply the concept to your workflows by simply asking agents to log what context files they used. We do this in our posthog monorepo PR template, which prompts agents to name any skills invoked. We’ve seen other agents use this information to catch and fix skill inconsistencies, like in this PR where Claude found an issue while unblocking stalled ClickHouse cleanup PRs. Try this: Agents face issues all the time. Ask them to provide feedback about your context with a structured prompt about any errors, inconsistencies, or failures they ran into. Over time, you can turn verified reports into a self-driving context system. Written by Jina Yoon, who would like a word with whoever coined the term “unhobbling.” Originally published in build mode, a free newsletter by PostHog.

post.author: Oren John
post.text: Yapping is talking on camera, just an iPhone, no fancy camera, and to start at least, no graphics. And despite how simple it sounds, it’s become the primary mode of business communication, personal brand building, and audience development in 2025. I published a full YouTube on this, and I want to give you the distilled version because I think it’s one of the most slept-on way to start participating in the creator economy right now. Why this matters more than most people realize The number one benefit I got from starting to make content wasn’t the followers or the revenue. It was becoming a better communicator. Thinking about what message I’m trying to get across, how to dismantle the objections someone has before I even say the main point, how to carry someone from where they are to where I want them to be. I cannot overstate the power making hundreds of videos gives you in helping communicate in all aspects of life The three formats worth knowing - Standard yap: sitting, iPhone, captions. That’s it. - Walking or car yap: more candid, more like a FaceTime. Harder to start with because there are too many variables, but useful once you have reps. - Graphic yap: you overlay images or video over your footage to keep attention. Shoot for one visual roughly every two seconds. This is the format that performs best at scale (templates below) - Notebook yaps: You can also use a notebook or whiteboard to help facilitate the conversation with notes and frameworks written out you reference The five frameworks that make up 90% of good yap content - Strong take: say something is the best or worst and defend it. Forces conviction and generates response. - Strong take into education: use the take as a hook, pivot immediately into the breakdown. That’s how you avoid being clickbait without sacrificing attention. - Small epiphany: the relatable observation. “Have you ever noticed...” builds camaraderie faster than almost anything. - Humor: a bit, a critique, a funny scenario. Underrated when you have a voice for it. - Story time: a thing that happened, told as a narrative. Oldest format in the world for a reason. Two script styles to start with: The yap map Every day, before you scroll, spend a few minutes mapping what happened. Meetings that surfaced good questions, conversations from lunch, ideas that came up in the shower, things you saw in your feed that you had a reaction to. Your goal is three to five ideas a day. Not fully formed scripts. Just prompts. You’ll be surprised how fast that list gets unwieldy. The one tactical thing most people skip Redo your opening at the end of the session. By the time you’re done recording, you’re warmed up. Go back and shoot the intro again. It’s almost always better. The barrier to starting has never been lower. The ceiling on what talking into your phone can become has never been higher. post.author: Seema Amble
post.text: The bullish case for incumbent systems of record is that AI makes systems of record get more important, not less. Why? Because in theory the customer can now pipe the system’s data into Claude or Codex and skip the AI-native app. As agents do more work through these systems, the data and actions they control become more valuable. An incumbent system of record plus a general agent (or an agent built by the incumbent) therefore might be enough to get the work done. This is what Salesforce just announced in partnership with Anthropic: Claudeforce lets you work with the Salesforce CRM from inside Claude without having to open Salesforce (or so they claim!). The argument is partly correct. The incumbents aren’t sitting idly. The incumbents have an incentive to control and charge for access to their data, and now to push their own agents forward too. We’re already seeing incumbents market products that move from simply storing information toward doing more of the work itself. Docusign’s Iris reviews contracts, Atlassian’s Rovo aims to resolve and route requests, and Klaviyo’s Composer builds campaigns and assesses marketing performance. These products move incumbents beyond the “slap on a chatbot” strategy and into taking action. At the same time, Claude is starting to coordinate work across applications, making it possible for general-purpose agents to act as a layer above the incumbents. Claudeforce shows what that can look like: Claude can become the front door to the job while Salesforce still controls the underlying CRM data and actions. The interface and the system of record look like they're unbundling, creating an opening for AI-native startups to rebundle around the job. So where can startups still compete? The vertical AI-native company has to win through focus. It has to perform a specific cross-system job better than an incumbent’s purpose-built agent or a general-purpose agent like Claude, which will be able to reconstruct it from the underlying tools. Focus can earn the vertical startup deeper access, a deliberate data asset, more specific context, and a learning loop that builds a better understanding over time of what good work looks like for a given job.

post.author: Pascio -
post.text: How I went from burning $9,000 on a failed dropshipping store to building a $1M+ solo business, and why I’m now starting a newsletter called Side Quests. Hi, I am Pascio. Today, over 370,000 cool people follow my stuff across the internet, and because they do, I’ve made over $1M in personal profit from the businesses I built off the back of that, mostly by myself, and always with my laptop and a (not always so fast) WiFi connection. For most of that time, I’ve done it being 100% faceless online. To properly kick off my first real side quest, my newsletter Side Quests, I figured a proper reintroduction was overdue. Now I know there are many of you reading this who have followed me since the good old days when I was selling Notion templates, some even tracing back to early 2021. Then there are others who found me through some random viral tweet or Instagram post after that, and probably also a few who have absolutely no idea who I am or why this article is popping up on their timeline. So allow me to take you back to the beginning. We’ll start by taking a quick trip down memory lane so you understand how I ended up where I am, but even more importantly, I'll share what I’m doing next (and why that specifically matters to you). Because lately I’ve found myself back in the very part of internet businessing that I enjoy most: chasing internet rabbit holes, clicking a ton of buttons, building weird shit, and seeing if any of it turns into good ol’ cold hard American dollar bills. Also summarizes pretty well what this newsletter is going to be about. More on that in a second. It all started with a sticky note About four years ago, I wrote a list of my top goals on yellow sticky note. Later as I got started with my online business, I turned those goals into a tweet and posted it publicly on X for some of that good ol’ juicy accountability: Admittedly, I still go back and look at that very tweet every once in a while. And more impressively, less than a year after posting the tweet, I had already checked off the first three goals on that list. I am still working on the fourth to this day. Before all this, there was very little evidence that any of it was going to happen in the first place if I’m being completely honest. See, I was stuck in this soul-draining 9-to-5 job where I was being forced (or, I mean, I did it willingly, but you know what I mean), to call strangers on the phone all day to try and sell them things they didn’t really want in the first place. If you’ve ever done any type of outbound sales or telemarketing, you know what I’m talking about when I say “soul-draining”. Now as a result of the crippling depression that was creeping up on me, I spent most of my free time trying to figure out how the hell people made money online. I tried a lot of things over the years. One of my earliest genius business ideas was dropshipping women’s clothes. The rationalization on this was very real, and it was simply because my girlfriend was spending lots of money buying clothes every month, so I reasoned with myself that this niche would definitely be the one to make me filthy rich. Oh boy, had I only known what I was in for… I ended up burning around $9,000 running paid ads before eventually accepting that I had created a remarkably efficient system for sending money from my bank account directly to Facebook, and not so much a business that got me paid (lol). After that experiment, I had no more money to play with. So I decided to go all in on content, because, well… it was free to create and post. Problem was that I had never created content before and I had no idea what to create it about, so again, my master rationalization skills came into play when I woke up one day and realized that I could just make a page and talk about my goals. So, as you know, my goal was to get rich and the result was an Instagram account called “The $1M Project”. The concept was… exactly what it sounds like. I was going to publicly document my journey to making a million dollars. And so I began. I made lots of content. The actual making money part proved… slightly more difficult. For around three years, that was more or less my relationship with online business. I would discover something, become convinced I had finally figured it out, spend weeks or months working on it, and eventually move on to the next idea when I failed epicly. Dropshipping. Instagram pages. Content. Random business models. Whatever rabbit hole looked promising that month. I had plenty of ambition and very little to show for it. So, eventually, I gave up entirely. I decided to just get better at my job. And so I began climbing the corporate ladder instead. I studied sales, improved my skills, closed more deals and got promotion after promotion. Eventually I realized that while the money got better, the depression didn’t. So I turned to self improvement as the solution. If I couldn’t change my life situation, well, the very least I could do was hit the gym. That journey led me to the most random thing of all times: Notion. ♡ Quick note: I write 1-2 letters/week just like this in Side Quests, my newsletter where I cover the products, prototypes, launches, growth experiments, weird ideas, and whatever I’m currently trying to figure out. Subscribe here to receive the next letter for free. The strangest thing changed my life entirely As I got deeper into the self dev space, I ended up with my life organized in these neat Google Drive folders. One for each, Health, Wealth, Happiness. You know the drill. And I was proud of this system I’d built. So proud that one day I showed it to my brother who was a university student and an an avid user of Notion. So he asked me, “why don’t you use Notion for this instead of Google Drive?” I’d never heard of Notion, but gave it a shot and one weekend later, I was knee deep. I got completely sucked into it, and started engaging in Notion communities. Eventually along the way, I came across people that were making surprisingly good money selling templates for it. That caught my attention specifically. Because if they could do it… why couldn’t I? The business model was equally attractive. There was almost nothing standing between me and the customer. I could build the product myself, put it on the internet, find people who wanted it, and keep most of the money I made for myself. So I started a faceless Twitter account from zero and began posting about Notion. My early tweets got something like two likes each, and I remain fairly confident that both of them were from my mom (thanks mom!) At the same time, I spent hours studying other successful creators trying to understand what people actually needed and would pay for. So I made systems for productivity, goals, businesses, habits, planning, and basically every other part of life people apparently wanted to organize inside a database. While everyone shipped a template a month, I was launching one every week. The first $5 I ever made online came from my first launch. And I use the word “launch” generously. It looked ridiculous compared with how I (or half of Tech Twitter) would launch something today but still, someone bought it. And then someone else. And another person. And another. Before I knew it, I had made $200 over the course of a few days. Pocket change, sure. But life-changing in the sense that it changed my life trajectory. And so, my account slowly grew, my products got better each time, and the income started growing at a compounding rate alongside it. After around six months of hustling and bustling (while still working that 9-5), I hit my first $2,000 month. Then I did it again the month after. And again the next month. At that point I quit my job and just went all in. Everyone around me thought I had lost it. Understandable. Because from the outside, I had given up a stable, well paying job, with another promised promotion just about to hit + the yearly 0.5% raise kicking in, … to spend my days tweeting anonymously from a cartoon character profile about a productivity app and selling digital planners to strangers on the internet. I sounded ridiculous. But from where I was sitting, it felt like I had finally found something with momentum after years of trying and failing at everything. The five bucks kicked things off. The $200 launch made me believe it was possible and the $2k months were the nail in the coffin that told me THIS WAS IT: my way out. So naturally, I wanted to see how far I could take it. Turns out people really wanted their lives organized After quitting my job, I now had 24/7 to ship products and write tweets. And now that I think about that, that right there, that paragraph, is basically the one-sentence secret to succeeding in an online business with zero prior experience: Ship products & write tweets 24/7. My little internet business selling cute Notion templates eventually scaled to $300,000 in profits. And it was still just me, my laptop and Twitter. The more interesting part was what started happening next. My Twitter audience kept growing and my email list along with it. And for every new person who entered my world, the next launch became a little easier and more profitable. Eventually I realized that the templates were only one part of the equation. The real asset I was building underneath it all was distribution. Once I understood that, I started stacking other things on top of what I already had. I built info products. I ran mentorships. I began closing high-ticket clients. I did partnerships and collaborations. I started playing with software, investing, doing acquisitions, and other small and (often weird) internet businesses. Some things worked incredibly well. Others quietly disappeared and shall never be spoken of again. Over time, that $300k from selling templates eventually crossed $1 million in total profit. And somehow, after all of that growth, I am still sitting here happily working from my laptop without a giant organization around me. Notion kickstarted the thing. Twitter and email scaled it. And everything I learned along the way then opened up a much larger playground. A playground that I genuinely believe everyone should get a chance to play on. ♡ Quick note: I write 1-2 letters/week just like this in Side Quests, my newsletter where I cover the products, prototypes, launches, growth experiments, weird ideas, and whatever I’m currently trying to figure out. Subscribe here to receive the next letter for free. The fine print I think we can agree that the clean version of this story sounds pretty sweet. It’s also the one I tell at dinner tables and cocktail parties when people ask me what I do and I answer “online business” and they look at me with these weird eyes waiting for me to elaborate. But you and both know that it’s really just the nice wrapper: I discovered Notion, started a Twitter account, sold some templates, built an audience, quit my job, and eventually made more than $1 million online. When you actual unpack it by zooming out a bit, the timeline is much uglier. I spent 3 years trying random shit online, failing most of it. I burned thousands of dollars. I spent hours and hours making content nobody cared about. And even then, my ambition started way before any of those failed business attempts. This is equally important because I have that same tendency today. I get curious about something, go too deep, start building, and occasionally emerge on the other side with an actual business. The cool thing is that because I’ve already laid the groundwork, I have a lot more leverage to take bets now: I have an audience. I have distribution. I have capital. I have experience. And even cooler, now AI has made it possible for a non-techy guy like me whose only coding skill is Notion formulas, to build things I would have needed a team for a few years ago. Which makes this a very fun time to start experimenting again, which brings me to… Welcome to Side Quests You’re reading Side Quest #1 of Side Quests. My newest lil’ project. See, over the last few years, Pascio became associated with the things I had already built. I became “The Notion Guy”, which kinda boxed me in and limited my curiosity from exploring beyond it. Today, I’m already experimenting and testing and fooling around, chasing internet rabbit holes and clicking a whole bunch of buttons to make money appear. I want Side Quests to be the newsletter that documents that, WHILE it happens. The easiest way I can describe it is this: Side Quests is my weekly field log from the trenches. I’ll share the businesses I’m building, products and prototypes I’m shipping, launches, growth experiments, acquisitions, weird ideas, numbers, failures, and whatever I’m currently trying to figure out as I go. Occasionally, a very stupid side quest turns into something that actually makes money. That is the fun part. There are plenty of places online where you can read the polished case study six months later, once somebody knows which decisions were smart and which details should conveniently disappear from the story. Here, I want to write while I’m still figuring it out. If I start something on Monday, I might tell you about it on Friday. If I spend money buying some strange internet asset, you’ll get the numbers. If I launch something and nobody cares, that can make the newsletter too, so we can all analyze why it wen’t wrong (after we stop collectively crying about it of course). And if an experiment suddenly takes off and starts printing dough, you’ll see what happened before I have time to rewrite the story into some genius master plan. You’ll probably notice a few recurring themes in this newsletter: Profit & Prototypes will cover the things I’m actually building and my tests to see whether anyone wants to pay for them. Build Logs will go deeper into active projects, what shipped, what broke, what changed, and where I’m taking them next. Internet Experiments will be the stranger stuff: distribution ideas, viral mechanics, new channels, weird websites, growth loops, and ideas I’m testing because I want to know what happens when I play with different variables. I’ll also share the economics when it matters, because why not? Revenue, costs, traffic, users, valuations, prices, whatever gives you the full picture. And there will inevitably be rabbit holes that begin with me thinking, “huh, that’s interesting,” and end three days later with twelve browser tabs open and a half-built company. Those probably deserve their own category, but rest assured, I shall definitely let you know about those too, so you can avoid wasting time and have me do it for you! I already have a new side quest A few days ago, I started building an Apple Watch app. The original thought was simple. I use different AI agents for different parts of my life and work, and I wanted a way to speak to them directly from my wrist without constantly pulling out my phone. So I started coding it. You can see some of that here: I have no idea yet where it ends up. It could become a proper product. It could lead me into a much bigger idea. It could end up in the enormous graveyard of things I found fascinating for four days before becoming fascinated by something else. Either way, that process is exactly what belongs here. I have a bunch of these experiments going at any given time. Software, content systems, acquisitions, little internet businesses, distribution plays, AI tools, and other things that probably make more sense once I have spent an unreasonable amount of time explaining them. Side Quests gives me somewhere to document all of it. And hopefully, seeing it will help you too whether it’s you seeing what to avoid, getting motivated or just copying my moves (permission granted!) One more important note There is one other thing I want to explain, because I’m increasingly getting questions about the difference of Pascio vs. Pascal. @IAmPascio (this faceless brand) is the builder side. That is where my side quests live. I build things, launch things, experiment, share numbers, chase opportunities, and generally use whatever leverage I have accumulated to see what I can make happen on the internet. This newsletter, and generally the Pascio brand, belongs to that world. @CreatorPascal (the real me) is my personal brand. This is where I go deeper and zoom out on the bigger picture of what building a 7-figure one person internet empire really is like. I recently renamed that newsletter Internet Leverage. The question behind it is something I spend a lot of time thinking about: What becomes possible when one person suddenly has access to distribution, software, AI, capital and a global market? Over there, I write longer essays about one-person businesses, attention as an asset, AI as leverage, internet-native wealth, ambition, culture and philosophy. More broadly, I’m interested in what happens as technology rewires how we work, think and live, and how you can use those shifts to get ahead. Some of those essays are practical field guides. Others are me following an idea until I understand it better. For whoever reads it, the end goal is giving them an edge. A way to learn the new rules of internet business while everyone else is still playing by the old ones, spot opportunities earlier, make better bets, and compound that advantage across work, money and life. That is Internet Leverage by Pascal. Side Quests by Pascio is much closer to the ground. One is where I think through the larger ideas and try to make sense of where all of this is going and what I’m learning from it in real-time. The other is where I open the laptop and actually start fucking around with it and showing you what happens when you do. And I think it’s a pretty genius move, because they feed each other naturally. The things I build give me new ideas to think about. The things I think about usually give me another excuse to build something. It turns out my business and my personality have basically become an infinite side-quest generator. So... what happens now? I genuinely don’t know. That is partly why I wanted to start this first newsletter sidequest. I’m in a very different position from the guy who was desperately trying to make his first few dollars online. I have distribution, capital, skills, an audience, and most importantly, access to technology that lets one person do things that would have required an entire team back when I started. I still have the same itch to see what happens if I follow an interesting idea far enough. Maybe the next side quest becomes another $300,000 template business (I heard Framer templates should be pretty profitable these days?) Maybe it becomes software (maybe another AI Head of Content like Stanley?) Maybe I buy something (so far, I’ve only sold some of my businesses, never bought). Or maybe I build something so stupid that the only responsible thing to do is send you an email about how badly it failed so you can avoid it at all costs. If you ask me, either of those outcome sounds far more interesting than pretending I already know the ending. So a few times a week, I’ll come back here and tell you what I’ve been building, testing, launching, buying, breaking, learning, and making money from. You’ll see the process while it is still messy + the numbers + the failures along the way. And, if history is any indication of whether I’ll succeed, well, I’m a strong believer that least a handful of these ridiculous rabbit holes should eventually turn into something that can fund my new IRL garden project (srsly, I need me some more tomato plants, the first one I just planted produced… 2 tomatoes). post.author: Alex Lieberman
post.text: This intern 6x'd her company's website traffic with an AI content machine called BlogEO. The big f*cking problem - Blog had almost no real measurement - Insights lived in ~5 places (GSC, Semrush, PostHog, Sanity, prior run snapshots) so nobody joined the data - ~70% of traffic came from 14 posts; ~50% from just 5 - Top SEO posts were often invisible to LLMs (AEO gap) Step 1: Run the AI audit - Pulls those five sources into one view - Content hygiene scan first: broken links, positioning drift, deprecated products - Broken-link fixes use @browserbase's fetch API to find the right replacement - Broken links + missing SEO fields can auto-publish (no human gate) - Scores every post into a ranking / opportunity queue - Flags the top ~15 for deeper fact-check + SEO verification - Drafts surgical edits (small, intentional) and stores each suggestion - Edits stay small on purpose. Most posts were handwritten; don’t paste AI voice over human voice - High-leverage changes: SEO title, meta description, swap a link - 28-day cooldown after changes so GSC has time to catch up (no thrashing the same post) Step 1b: Score post opportunities • Unit of opportunity = clicks • Click recovery: if clicks fell hard vs the last ~28 days, that lost volume is opportunity. Real click loss beats any estimate and jumps the queue. • CTR gap: compare your CTR at a given position to what page-one / peers get at that same spot. Gap × impressions ≈ clicks you’re leaving on the table. (Alex’s example: position 9 averages ~5% CTR; you’re at 1% → the 4-pt delta is the opportunity.) • Rank upside: if you’re on page 2/3, estimate clicks if you moved to page 1 / to the average for that better position. (Her example: post at 9.4 with a pink-dot underperform → ~7,400 click opportunity if it hit the average for that position.) • Queue, then spend: every post gets a cheap score; only the top ~15 get the expensive fact-check / deep SEO pass (token control). Near-invisible / irrelevant queries don’t score high on purpose. Step 3: Avoid AI slop - New posts aren’t a firehose ideas surface as drafts, ~once a week - Ignore / skip is a first-class option if the query isn’t worth owning - Quality gate before anything ships - Slack card shows who approved and who published — accountability stays with a person - Human pride > “we shipped another AI blog” Step 4: Run the full blog machine - Weekly cadence in Slack: Monday = content generation, Tuesday = audit (plus on-demand “audit this page now”) - Agent (BB) has skills: audit, strategy, writing, generate...always drafts suggestions first - Agent has no write path to live content until a human clicks - Slack cards: Approve / Edit / Skip / Discard → only then does it hit the CMS - Approved edits + outcomes land in internal DBs (including what never shipped) - Near-miss queries (show up in search, no targeted page) feed the generator side The results Search impressions: +5.8x Page-one queries: +9.8x Avg blog position: page 2 → page 1 Massive shoutout to @harsehaj for the amazing internship project & masterclass in AI-powered AEO/SEO!

title: I have 15 client folders open in my terminal right now. Opening the 15th cost…
note: @Kenny_GTM: I have 15 client folders open in my terminal right now. Opening the 15th cost me about what the 2nd did, and that single fact is the whole difference between a services-as-software company and an agency paying for a Claude subscription. The pitch is the half everyone has heard…

post.author: Kenny Damian
post.text: I have 15 client folders open in my terminal right now. Opening the 15th cost me about what the 2nd did, and that single fact is the whole difference between a services-as-software company and an agency paying for a Claude subscription. The pitch is the half everyone has heard. You price a result instead of hours, you say software does the work, the client signs. That part is easy, which is why the model spread so fast. The second half is where it comes apart, and it never comes apart loudly. It shows up as a GTM engineer asking in Slack what a client's ICP is, 4 months after kickoff. Or a scoring model getting rebuilt from memory, because the good version lives in another account and nobody remembers which one. By client 3 you are hand-building what you already hand-built for client 1, charging software prices for it, and hiring your way back into the business you were trying to leave. So here is the test. What does it cost you to open client folder 15 compared to folder 2? Roughly the same means software is genuinely doing the delivery. Anything more and you are running an agency with a much harder story to tell. At Frontal we have done this work across 275 companies and the same thing is true every time: companies buy the tools and cannot make them run. The 6 systems below are what keep folder 15 cheap. Worth building at 2 clients, and at 15 there is no business without them. By the end of this, you'll know: The 1 file that lets someone take over a client account in minutes instead of asking 3 people what the ICP is What to keep isolated per client and what to share across all of them, and why cross-client bleed is the hardest bug to spot The procedures worth writing once, including the scoring model that removes roughly 80% of manual sorting Which 4 jobs still need a human, and the 1 workflow you should never put inside a folder None of this needs a developer. It does need your own API keys, and something will break on the first run of every build. That is the honest boundary. The rest is copyable as written. A note on the order. Each system has a client number on it. That is roughly the point where not having it starts costing you real hours. Build them in sequence and you pay for each one just before you need it. 1. The folder boundary Starts costing you at: client 2. 1 folder per client. Its own context, its own API keys, its own history. Nothing crosses between them unless I move it across on purpose. This is the boring one and nobody wants to start here. Start anywhere else and you will spend a month debugging the wrong layer. Inside each folder I use the WAT structure. Workflows are markdown instructions. The agent is Claude Code. Tools are the scripts that execute actions. 3 folders, and every new file has an obvious home. At the root sits CLAUDE.md. This is the system prompt for the project. Without it Claude is generic. With it, Claude is an expert in that client's workflows, tools and data. Keep it under 200 lines. I have spent 600+ hours inside Claude Code and that cap is the single rule I have never regretted setting. Past 200 lines it stops working as a system prompt and turns back into a document, and nobody reads documents properly, including the model. I decide what earns a place in those 200 lines before I build anything else in the folder. Whatever does not fit has to live somewhere on purpose, which is what the next 2 systems are for. What breaks without it: client 2's positioning turns up in client 1's copy and nobody notices for a week. There is no error message for this. The output reads clean and is just wrong. 2. The per-client context file Starts costing you at: person 2 on the account. Every client gets a context.md. ICP, offer, personas, what is working, what is not. Before we built this at Frontal, we had normal agency chaos. Good ideas lived in Slack. Copy wins were shared in our #random channel, literally. Research stayed in 1 person's head. New hires relearned old lessons. With per-client context files, a GTM engineer picks up any account in minutes. No more "let me check with sales" for basic context. 1 rule matters more than the file itself: rank your sources. The ICP doc, the intelligence store and last quarter's campaign notes will eventually disagree with each other. Decide which one wins before an agent runs, not after it has written 40 emails on the losing one. GitHub became our source of truth for all of it. That sounds like housekeeping until output changes on an account and you can diff the context file to find out exactly why. What breaks without it: onboarding a new person costs you about as much as onboarding a new client. That is the exact cost you were trying to get rid of. 3. The skills library Starts costing you at: client 5. Around folder 5 you notice you have written the same procedure 5 times, each version slightly different, and you cannot remember which one was the good one. That is the signal to stop and build this. A skill is an instruction file that teaches Claude how to do 1 specific GTM task. Claude loads only what is relevant to the job in front of it. I open-sourced the 15 skills we run across 70+ clients. 5 pillars, roughly 4,200 lines of methodology. The internal set is where the compounding happens: Copywriting. Our winning cold email frameworks, written down. TAM scoring. 80 to 100 point scoring models. Contact enrichment. A 3-layer waterfall. Campaign delivery. A 9-phase checklist. Signal detection. 30 intent signals across 4 tiers. Clay, database search and RevOps skills for every CRM we touch. 1 engineer writes the skill once and every folder calls the same copy of it. This is the first system on the list that makes folder 15 cheaper than folder 5 instead of just holding it level. Here is what one of them actually contains. The ICP skill clones a client's ICP from their closed-won customers in 6 steps: Pull closed-won domains. The last 30 to 50 deals from their CRM. Domains only. These companies converted, paid and did not churn, which is better signal than any persona doc. Find lookalikes. Drop the seed domains into CompanyEnrich's similar-companies API. Vector search runs across 30M+ companies and returns 50 matches per seed. 10 closed-won domains in, 500+ ranked lookalikes out. Enrich with signals. Same tool, layered. Funding rounds mean new budget. Leadership moves mean a new buyer in the seat. Hiring spikes in target roles mean the team is expanding. Tech stack changes mean intent for adjacent tools. These become the relevance hooks for step 6. Score and tier. Send each account through a classification prompt in Claude, using closed-won plus signal data as the rubric. Tier 1 is strong fit with an active signal. Tier 2 is strong fit, no signal yet. Tier 3 is adjacent fit, watchlist. Roughly 80% of the manual sorting goes away here. Enrich contacts. CompanyEnrich, Prospeo and FullEnrich. People search across 170M+ profiles for the right titles, then a waterfall through multiple providers for verified emails. Personalize per tier. 1 prompt per Tier 1 account using its signal context. Templated hooks for Tier 2 with a single variable swap. High-volume sequences for Tier 3. Outreach intensity matches the tier: call plus LinkedIn plus email for Tier 1 through Nooks, lemlist and Instantly. LinkedIn plus email for Tier 2. Email only for Tier 3. That is 1 skill, written once, called by every folder, and fixed in 1 place on the day it turns out to be wrong. 4. The connection layer Starts costing you at: the first time an agent describes last month's pipeline back to you. MCP servers. 1 connection and Claude controls the whole tool, endpoints and parameters included. The 10 I would connect for any GTM team: Notion, Slack, n8n, HubSpot, Apollo, Instantly, Firecrawl, Fireflies, GitHub and ClickUp. At Frontal the working set across accounts is Instantly, Fireflies, Notion, Clay, Apollo and Attio. Setup is 1 line per tool. About 5 minutes each. That is the whole install cost for the layer that makes Claude Code an operating system instead of a chatbot. A few of these earn their place on day 1. With Fireflies connected, Claude can search every meeting you have ever had and pull transcripts, action items and summaries without anyone opening a recording. Instantly means launching campaigns and reading analytics from the terminal. And n8n lets Claude build, test and debug automations without you opening the UI at all. What breaks without it: the agent has all of your instructions and none of your live state. What comes out is fluent, well-structured, and describes a pipeline that stopped being true 3 weeks ago. That is much harder to catch than something that simply breaks. 5. The data layer Starts costing you at: client 9 or so, the first time someone asks how an account is doing and the answer is a manual report. Supabase underneath everything. All TAM lists, contacts, campaigns and performance snapshots in 1 database. Campaign performance gets tracked daily on its own, so you can look at a trend without anyone pulling a report for it. The part that matters for delivery cost: every engineer queries the same data. 1 person's work becomes available to everyone else without a handoff meeting, a Loom, or a Slack thread nobody reads. Deploy the scheduled pieces to a cloud runner and pay only when they run. Trigger on a schedule or a webhook. It runs while you sleep, which is the only realistic way to get a daily snapshot across 15 accounts. Before you deploy anything here, run a security review. 1 prompt: check for exposed API keys and vulnerabilities. It takes about 30 seconds and it is the cheapest insurance in this stack. 6. The intelligence store Starts costing you at: the moment client 10 relearns what client 3 already proved. Every campaign insight gets logged. Which copy angles worked and which did not, which personas responded best, which segments outperformed. Stored per target type, per market, per ICP. Before writing new copy, Claude checks what is already proven for that specific segment. That is the whole loop. Across the agency that store now holds 11,000 campaigns, 132,000 snapshots and 30+ clients. When 1 engineer finds a winning angle on a Tuesday, every other account can be using it by Thursday. The other 5 systems exist to stop your delivery cost climbing as you add clients. This is the only place in the stack where what you deliver gets better while nobody is working on it. What the 6 actually buy you 500+ AI workflows across 70+ clients. 37 agents running for a $7M ARR business. Of those 37, about 6 changed how we operate day to day, and pre-call research is the clearest one: a full brief in 90 seconds that used to take a rep 15 minutes of manual digging. At campaign level it looks like this. Claude Code reads the Instantly API docs straight out of the project folder, hits the Apollo API, and pulls 153 contacts in about 90 seconds. I run those through a waterfall, Wiza then FullEnrich then Prospeo, and end up with 149 verified emails. On a full waterfall, coverage pushes past 90%. Campaign live in Instantly. Anyone can do that once, in 1 folder, on a good day. It turns into a business when the procedure was written down once and folder 15 calls the exact same copy of it. The 4 jobs that still need a human API keys. You add your own, per folder, every time. There is no version of this where that gets automated away, and you would not want one. The debugging pass. Something breaks on the first run of every build. Claude will investigate the error, fix the code and update the workflow so it does not break the same way twice. You still have to be there for the first one. The cut. Tiering removes roughly 80% of the manual sorting. The last 20% is a judgment call about which accounts do not deserve a send at all, and that call has revenue attached to it. The call. The pre-call brief lands in Slack in 90 seconds. It does not run the meeting. The one workflow you should not put in a folder This whole stack is built for individual-level work, and that is also where it stops. I am the only person on those 15 accounts, and that is a large part of why it holds together. Put the same 15 folders on 5 laptops with 5 operators and you no longer have a system. You have 5 people guessing which version of a skill is the current one. So keep the revenue-critical, team-level workflow out of it. If you build a RevOps flow that pulls from the CRM, checks the data is fresh and pushes updates back, that flow cannot live locally on someone's machine. It needs a monitored home in the cloud where the whole team can see what is running and what failed at 3am. Build the folder stack for work that 1 person owns end to end. Anything the whole revenue team depends on belongs somewhere they can all watch it.

post.author: Jay Yang
post.text: I’ve helped launch a book to become a New York Times best-seller. I’ve helped another break a Guinness World Record for the fastest-selling non-fiction book in under 24 hours. My own books have become Amazon best-sellers. I’ve worked behind the scenes with some of the biggest personal brands in business, and grown my own audience to over 500,000 followers. I only say all that for people who don’t know who I am or why they should keep reading. Because in this essay, I’m going to share 6 years of marketing advice: the philosophy behind everything I do, for clients and for myself. Contents - 13 min read - What is marketing? - Future demand vs. current demand - How to create future demand - Why brand matters - The content multiplication system - How to capture current demand - How they play together - If you want to apply this to your own business - Recap What is marketing? Marketing is the process of reaching and converting customers. If you can get in front of the right people, and then convince them to buy your thing, you win. Why is marketing important? When you have more demand than supply, it’s hard not to win. The mental model I like to give people is this: imagine I tripled the number of leads coming into your business. What would happen? If you’re a decent business owner, your business would probably grow. In an age where AI can create pretty much anything, the ability to create distribution, to make yourself oversubscribed with demand, is only getting more powerful. When you do marketing right: - Strangers DM you asking about a problem you posted about weeks ago - Prospects bring up your posts on calls before you even pitch - Other founders start asking how you’re getting inbound - Your best customers found you through a post, not a referral So that’s step one: understanding what marketing is. Step two is realizing there are actually 2 types of demand. Future demand vs. current demand What’s the likelihood you buy a new car in the next 2 weeks? Probably low. What about in the next 20 years? Probably a lot higher. My goal isn’t to right hook you right now. It’s to increase your affinity to my brand so that when you enter the buying window, you think of my brand first. There are 2 types of demand: current demand and future demand. Current demand is getting you to use our product or service now. Future demand is the amount of possible demand your brand could have in the future. Most people view marketing as capturing current demand, because it’s easy to track and attribute, so we allocate more of our time there. Traditional marketers call this direct response marketing. Great marketers view marketing as capturing current demand and creating future demand. Not everything that can be measured matters. Not everything that matters can be measured. Let’s talk about creating future demand first, then capturing current demand. How to create future demand Future demand is the byproduct of brand. Brand is the association between two things: one you know about, and one you don’t know about yet. Branding is teaching. If I point at a tree and say “tree,” kids will associate the tree with the sound “tree.” Bad branding is when your audience makes the associations for you. Good branding is when your audience associates you with the things you want to be associated with. So ask yourself: what do you need to be associated with for your audience to want to buy from you? My favorite way to build these associations is a framework I call PTL: Power, Trust, Likeness. Power Power is your ability to affect change in the world, showing that you have what others want. That could be money, cars, a mansion. It could be your network, your skill set, your results. Power is relative. A bartender has power in the bar, because they control who gets a drink and how fast. Once they step outside the bar, that power is gone. A famous investor has power in a meeting with founders, because the founders want their money. But that same investor has low power compared to the coach at a kids’ soccer game. You can show power 2 main ways: - Verbally (“Last year my portfolio did $250m in revenue”) - Visually (a picture of your big building) Try this What do your customers want, both internally and externally? Trust Trust is the belief that following your direction will produce a good result. Trust comes from evidence. Belief without evidence is faith. Trust is built when I tell you to do something, you do it, and a good thing happens. Each time that happens, the likelihood you comply with me in the future goes up. Parents have high trust with their kids because they’ve spent years giving directions that produced good results. Eat your vegetables and you’ll grow. Wear sunscreen and you won’t burn. Don’t talk to strangers and you’ll stay safe. Martha Stewart has high trust with her audience because for decades she’s given step-by-step directions, her recipes, that produced good results in their kitchens. If you follow her cake recipe and it comes out right, the next time she shares a recipe, you’ll go grab your flour. Try this What step-by-step directions can you give your customers to get positive results? For example: - Use these 50 hooks in your content - Read this book on storytelling - Use this tool to automate posting your content Likeness Likeness is how similar you are to the person you’re trying to influence. In psychology, this is called the in-group effect. An in-group is a social group an individual identifies with. People show favoritism, trust, and empathy toward members of their in-group, and skepticism or bias toward people outside it. That similarity shows up 2 ways: - Physical attributes (how someone looks, how they dress, their age) - Values (what they believe, where they’re from, what they care about, how they speak) Try this What are your customers’ internal and external attributes? For example: ex-athletes who wear athletic clothing, mid-30s to 40s, work a 9-to-5, want to get back in shape, want to feel athletic and powerful, and want to take agency over their life. To build an influential brand, demonstrate those 3 things, power, trust, and likeness, over and over and over again. A note on going viral Going viral does matter. People often say you only need 1,000 true fans to make a living online. Sure, but your first 1,000 followers are not going to be your first 1,000 true fans. You’re probably going to have to get to 10,000 or 100,000 followers and nurture them into fans. There are 2 approaches: - Stay super niche, only talk about one thing, and become known for that one thing, only reaching the people who are interested in it right now - Be yourself, reach many people, educate them about your interests, raise their awareness level, and turn them into customers over time Personally, I’d rather build cities than one skyscraper. I think you have more fun, can do it for longer, and build a more durable brand. Why brand matters We all know a business survives because of one equation: LTV to CAC. Basically, how much does it cost to acquire a customer, and how much do you make from them over their lifetime? The best businesses have a high LTV:CAC ratio. You know what increases that ratio? Brand. On the CAC side: - Increases the number of leads you get (one piece of content can reach millions of people) - Increases the conversion rate of those leads (they feel like they already know, like, and trust you, they’re pre-sold) On the LTV side: - Customers are willing to pay more, buy more frequently, and stay longer (they give you the benefit of the doubt) And here’s a 201-level benefit for the more advanced business owners: brand also improves your LTGPPE-to-CAT ratio, your lifetime gross profit per employee versus your cost to acquire talent. You get more talent Higher-quality talent For cheaper That stay longer And are already pre-sold into your beliefs and values The content multiplication system What do all the top personal brands have in common? They’re prolific. I learned this lesson from Noah Kagan. When I was 17, I worked as his head of content. He’d always repeat this phrase: test, then invest. Our north star goal was growing his email newsletter ahead of his book launch. So we asked: of the platforms we’re posting on, which one is driving the most email subscribers? Why don’t we double down on that? On X, of the content we’re posting, which formats are driving the most email subscribers? Why don’t we double down on that? And if we’re going to double down, how do we test before we invest? We’d post tweets, see what worked, then expand the winners into Twitter threads. That’s how the content multiplication system was born. This is how I still run my content today: 1. I tweet 4 to 10 times a day (idea playground) 2. My AI assistant Stanley flags which tweets outperform our average 3. I take that tweet and find 4 to 5 others like it and post them as an Instagram carousel 4. I voice-note it, clean it up, and post it as a long-form article or LinkedIn post 5. If that article does well, I clean it up further and send it as a newsletter 6. If that newsletter does well, I turn it into a YouTube video 7. I take the audio and put it on Spotify and Apple Podcasts 8. I also repost my bangers every 90 days, and rewrite or remix them with other bangers to create new mega-bangers: - Same idea, new format - New idea, same format By year 5 or 6, you’re mostly playing your best hits, just like singers do. Now you have a compounding machine, and people call you lucky. Build a Hall of Fame Every week, run a T3B3. What were the top 3 pieces of content? What were the bottom 3? How do you double down on the ones that did well and cut what didn’t? The top 10% of everything you’ve ever posted goes into a doc: your Hall of Fame. What you rank them by depends on what you’re optimizing for. Save the hooks separately from the posts. That matters later. Keep a second list of your core ideas, the things you actually believe. His had 17. A few of them: - NOW, not HOW - Test, then invest - Persistence beats resistance - You only need to be right once to win - The best marketing is a great product - Never forget the taco (be weird, be you) - Say the same thing in a bunch of different ways Once you have your top posts, it’s about figuring out how to say the same thing in a bunch of different ways. I call this the 3Rs. 1/ Repost Repost your top posts every 90 days. People get weird about reposting. But less than half your audience saw it the first time, and the ones who did need to be reminded more than they need to be taught. Change the hook, change the image, modify the body, and post it again. 2/ Repurpose Test an idea as a tweet first. If it works, write it up as a longer post. Then record a podcast on it. Take the podcast, transcribe it, and write the transcript into the newsletter. The newsletter becomes a Twitter thread. The thread becomes a LinkedIn post. You only have to record once a week. Everything else comes out of that one recording. Then run 3 CTAs around every newsletter: - Pre-CTA the day before: “tomorrow we’ll talk about X.” - CTA the day it went out: “I just talked about this.” - Post-CTA the day after: “yesterday I talked about this.” 3/ Remix Remixing is taking two things that already worked and combining them into one new post. Every post has 2 jobs. The hook has to stop someone, and the body has to land. Most posts only do one of them well. So when you have a post where the idea landed but not many people saw it, and a hook from somewhere else that pulled a lot of people in, you put the hook on the post and both halves are already proven. If you master this skill, the world is yours. But making content is only half the equation. Now let’s talk about how to get paid today, how to capture current demand. How to capture current demand Organic content is great for creating future demand and getting people aware of you. Direct response, or ads, is where you right hook your audience. Organic content widens the outer circle, the number of people who are aware of you. Paid ads widen the inner circle, the number of people who actually buy from you. The goal of your content is to educate your audience about a problem they may have. The goal of your ads is to speak to the people who already have that problem. When you write ads, talk more about pain aversion than promise. If you can articulate someone’s pain better than they can, they’ll believe you have the ability to solve it. Focus on their pain, not your pitch. Here’s a pro tip: some of the best ads I’ve ever produced came from downloading all the sales calls of customers who bought our product and using AI to analyze why they bought. Then we used their exact words and said them back to the customer in the ads. So if they bought because they wanted: - More freedom to travel the world - A career with uncapped upside - More flexibility to be with their kids Then we’d say those things back to them in the ads: - “Are you a woman who wants more freedom to travel the world?” - “Are you tired of being overworked and underpaid, and want to finally be paid for your hard work?” - “Have you ever felt a little guilty for having to be at work while your kids get raised by a nanny?” That’s how you get the exact language your customers already use, and mirror it back to them. Hooks are the 80/20 of the ad. Battle-test your hooks by recording multiple, then kaleidoscoping them with a body. One tip we’ve found: specificity (like “$1m a year”) plus scarcity (like “invite to HQ for a private workshop”) wins. Where do winning hooks come from? - Your previous ads - Your free content - Other people’s ads - Other people’s free content - Platform-specific ad libraries The body of the ad, what I call the meat, usually falls into one of 3 buckets: - Testimonial ads (podcast style, parade of proof, lifecycle ad, raw testimonial, walk-and-talk rant style) - Education ads (like whiteboard explainer ads) - Story ads (lifestyle ads and straight storytelling) And the CTA needs to answer: - What to do - How to do it - When to do it - What they get for doing it - What happens next (optional) How they play together Brand makes the circle bigger. Direct response converts the 1%. It’s no longer organic versus paid. It’s explore with organic, exploit with paid. If you want to apply this to your own business A few questions worth sitting with: - If I tripled your leads, what would happen? - What do you need to be associated with? - How can you demonstrate power? What does your audience want, internally and externally? - How can you demonstrate trust? What step-by-step directions can you give them? - How can you demonstrate likeness? What are their internal and external attributes? - How are you going to leverage one piece of content into many? - What’s in your hall of fame? - Have you transcribed your sales calls to find out why people actually buy? - Have you built an empathy map? - What are your winning hooks? Recap There are 2 types of demand: current and future. To create future demand, demonstrate power, trust, and likeness. Brand improves your LTV to CAC. Use the content multiplication system to be prolific. Run ads that target pain to capture current demand. This is how you win in marketing in 2027 and beyond. Want to apply this to your business? Work with me→

post.author: chris
post.text: I'm starting this series because I wish I had something like this when I was trying to understand startup roles myself. Before we get into it, you might reasonably be asking: who is writing this? TLDR: After graduating, I was as an early-stage VC investor at @panachevc who then left to join @trynationgraph. a Series A startup backed by @Menloventures to do growth/marketing. Seven months later, I got promoted, helped bring in hundreds of thousands of dollars in closed-won deals, generated millions in pipeline, and was recently featured by Clay as a GTM engineer to watch. This isn't to boast but to show you that anything is possible and you can also break into a startup too as someone non-technical. I'm still figuring it out but I ought to share some lessons on the way. In this series: I’m going to try to show you exactly what I would do if I had to start from zero again: Which roles I’d target and which exist. Which kinds of companies I’d go after. How I’d get their attention, and how I’d turn that attention into a job. Let's start with the basics and what roles exist. At most startups you should probably be either building or selling This is an oversimplification, but I think it's a useful way to think about most early-stage startups generally. At the beginning, a startup really needs to do two things: build something people want and figure out how to get people to buy it. If you're an engineer, the first path is fairly obvious. You can help build the product. If you're non-technical and early in your career, I think you should try to get as close as possible to the second. Help the company get customers. This doesn't mean every non-technical person needs to become part of the GTM team within the startup. As startups get into later stages, there are obviously many other important roles: account management, product managers, finance, operations, recruiting, chiefs of staff, and so on. But many of those roles become easier to break into once you have a few years of experience and a clearer skill set. This guide is specifically for someone coming out of school or with less than two years of experience who doesn't have much of a track record yet. At that stage, I think one of the easiest ways to make yourself valuable is to work on something the company cares about every single day: revenue. That could mean directly selling the product. It could mean generating pipeline for the sales team. It could mean creating content that brings people to the website. It could mean improving SEO, running events, making videos, building outbound campaigns, or automating parts of the entire process. The titles for these jobs can get confusing very quickly: sales, growth, community, marketing, demand gen, SDR, BDR, GTM engineering. When I was first looking at startup jobs, half of these sounded like completely different careers. But it's actually quite simple if you break it down. So what actually falls under GTM? The easiest way to simplify it is to think about it is to think about it is outbound and inbound GTM. Outbound means you go find the customer. You figure out which companies should buy your product, find the right people inside those companies, and try to start a conversation with them: Cold calling and cold email are the obvious examples, but it also includes prospecting, account research, list building, LinkedIn outreach, writing sequences, and all the work that goes into turning a company you've never spoken to into a sales opportunity. If you see an SDR or BDR role, this is generally the world you're entering. Inbound works in the opposite direction. Instead of going out and finding each customer, you're creating things that make potential customers find you. This is where a lot of what we traditionally call marketing sits: Writing content, making videos, working with UGC creators, publishing blog posts, improving the website, building landing pages, working on SEO/AEO, running events, creating case studies, and generally finding ways to get more of the right people interested in what you're building. If you see a founding Marketer, community, social media manager this is generally the direction you will be entering. Now the title "Growth" is no different, it just means you're living somewhere between the lines above or all of it at once depending on the company. More recently, there is another layer that sits across both of these: GTM engineering. Whatever you want to call it! You don't have to be an engineer to be a GTM engineer The name makes this role sound more intimidating than it is. At a basic level, this type of "engineering" work is using software, data, AI, and automation to make sales and marketing more effective. Contrary to popular belief you do not need to come from an engineering background or degree to do this role. Maybe your sales team is manually researching 100 accounts. You build a workflow that can research 10,000 (this is what @trynationgraph does if you sell to the government). Maybe you're manually finding the right person at every company before sending them an email. You create a system that automatically sends cold emails to website visitors. Maybe your marketing team is doing the same repetitive research every week. You automate their work. A few years ago, doing a lot of this would have required significantly more engineering help. That's changing quickly. Tools like @Clay and AI coding agents like @Claudeai have made it possible for people who aren't software engineers to build surprisingly sophisticated things. But there's an important distinction here: Not being an engineer doesn't mean you should be afraid of technical things. You don't need to learn how to build production level ready code. But you should know what GitHub is. You should understand the basics of pushing and pulling changes. You should be comfortable opening the terminal and using simple bash commands like cd and ls. You should understand your local file system and have a rough idea of how API/MCPs work. AI can increasingly handle the implementation. Your job is to understand the problem well enough to tell it what you want, give it the right context, recognize when it gives you something bad, and steer it toward something better. That's where taste becomes important. For a non-technical person entering startups today, I think that combination, first principles critical thinking, basic technical literacy, and taste, is incredibly powerful. Now that we've gone through the basics of the types of roles you should look for. Next, I'll talk about how to pick that startup and how to stand out to get the role. Till next time. With gratitude, Chris
