post.author: Shaan Puri
post.text: My friend came over yesterday and I could tell something was wrong. - his mom has a scary health issue - his own health has felt off for months (docs keep saying 'everything looks fine', but it's not) - wife is panicking googling his symptoms and seeing scary stuff On top of that, he felt like he was underperforming at work. None of these things, by themselves, were crushing. But all of them at once? Overwhelmed. And hte worst part of feeling overwhelmed isn't the feeling. it's feeling ashamed for feeling that way. Today, I sent him this email: Hey man— I’ve been thinking about our conversation. There are three things I want you to remember. 1. Remember: life is seasonal. When you’re in a bad season, your brain does this funny thing where it assumes, This is just life now. It isn’t. You’ve had seasons where everything was clicking. You’ve also had storms that, at the time, felt like they’d never end. But they did. This one will too. 2. Remember: there’s only one decision to make. When you have 1,000 things hitting you at once, it’s easy to get overwhelmed and overthink it. In reality, you only have 1 decision to make: Am I going to have a common reaction or uncommon response? “Reactions” are automatic. Impulsive. “Responses” are choices. You get to choose how you respond to the situation. When we’re in the gym lifting - those last 2 reps when our arms are shaking, there’s a reaction of “sh*t this is hard” and so you break form and rush it. But the response is to choose poise. Deep breath. Remind yourself these last few reps are where all the gains happen. So you slow down and finish strong. Most guys in your position will have a common reaction: You feel overwhelmed, then you feel sorry for yourself. You start avoiding the things you know you need to do, then you feel guilty because you’re avoiding them, which makes you even more overwhelmed. Round and round you go. You don’t need to have perfect responses 100% of the time. But if you can switch from a ‘common reaction’ to an ‘uncommon response’ 50-75% of the time, that changes everything. Life is either happening to you or for you. 3. Remember: control the controllables. The serenity prayer says: Grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change, the courage to change the things I can, and the wisdom to know the difference. A lot of your suffering right now is coming from trying to play God. You want to control your mom’s health, your health, your wife’s anxiety, what happens at work, and how everyone feels about all of it. You can’t. That’s not your job. Your job is to control the controllables: your actions. Fly back home. Show up with a cheerful attitude. Make the appointments with the doctors. Get good sleep. Control what you can control. Everything else you either let go of, or get dragged by. This experience is happening whether you like it or not. You’re going through the tunnel. The question isn’t whether you go through it. The question is how you go through it. Go through it well. —shaan P.S. go for a run I don’t have great ideas when I’m depressed. The first thing to do is change your state of mind. The fastest way to do that is an intense physical thing. Go sprint. Do pushups. Take a freezing shower. Get outside. Change the body first, then think. And when you come up with one good thing to do, do it immediately. Action creates momentum, and momentum makes the next action easier.

title: I hired one of our first employees at Bland to be an SDR. For several months he…
note: @zaygranet: I hired one of our first employees at Bland to be an SDR. For several months he did basically none of that, and I was working out how to let him go. What I didn't know was that he'd been quietly working three accounts himself. He'd decided that closing those three mattered more…

post.author: Isaiah Granet
post.text: I hired one of our first employees at Bland to be an SDR. For several months he did basically none of that, and I was working out how to let him go. What I didn't know was that he'd been quietly working three accounts himself. He'd decided that closing those three mattered more than the outbound I kept hounding him about. Then he closed our biggest deal, and then the next one (Everyone at Bland knows exactly who I'm talking about. He knows I'm writing this. He has not asked to read it first, which is very on brand.) He hasn't had a task assigned to him in a long time. He does more or less what he wants, and I'm fine with that. He figured out before I did that he'd rather catch the snitch than score hoops. He found his golden snitch I. The Rules In Quidditch, a goal is worth ten points. Catching the snitch is worth a hundred and fifty and ends the match. Fifteen goals at once, and no time for the other team to answer. Unless you're far enough behind, you've won. There are results like that at work. For an AE, there's a deal big enough to make the year's quota on its own. Close it and the question of whether you'll hit quota is settled. For an engineer, it might be cutting the cost of running the product enough to make the business profitable. For an FDE, getting a customer to expand from one team to the whole company. These aren't just unusually productive weeks. They're results big enough to settle the thing you were trying to accomplish. That's your snitch. You should know what it is. II. It Looks Like Work The chaser is visibly busy all match. The seeker is circling, looking, apparently doing nothing. If you didn't know the rules, you'd assume the chaser was the one earning their keep. That's why my hire looked like a problem. Outbound is countable. You can put it in a spreadsheet and review it Monday. Three accounts he was quietly working didn't show up anywhere until they closed. I wanted customers. I'd assigned him outbound because I thought that was how he'd help us get them. He'd found another way, and I was so busy checking whether he was doing what I'd asked that I nearly missed it. It's easy to make this mistake from either side. As an employee, you can spend your whole week responding to requests. There's always another one, and someone is usually pleased when you finish it. You can go a long time without asking what all this work is supposed to add up to. The snitch may never appear on your task list. Whoever writes the list may not have seen it either. III. It Feels Unfair Suppose you've been working hard, doing everything you're asked. A colleague seems to ignore half the assignments, spends months on something you barely understand, and then gets the praise and the freedom. You put in more hours. Why do they get to choose their own work? That reaction makes sense if you think the rewards are supposed to measure effort. We know what our own work cost us. We remember the weekends and the problems that ran long. We want those counted. But a hundred and fifty points are a hundred and fifty points. They don't become worth less because someone else worked harder for ten. If an engineer saves the company a million dollars in a month, spending six months on a feature doesn't necessarily make the feature more valuable. The effort was real. So was the million dollars. This is easier to understand when you're the customer. If someone fixes your problem in an hour, you don't wish they'd taken a week. It's also easier when you remember you're on the same team. You wouldn't want a teammate to pass up the snitch because you'd spent the afternoon scoring goals. You'd want them to catch it. And once someone has found and caught it a few times, giving them freedom is a fairly practical decision. They've shown they can identify something worth doing without waiting for you to assign it. You want them to keep doing that. IV. Finding It In Quidditch, you know what you're looking for. At work, figuring that out can be the hardest part. Try finishing this sentence: if I accomplish _____ in the next six months, it will be obvious I've done an exceptional job. The answer should describe a result. “Work on infrastructure” doesn't. “Cut the cost to serve each customer in half without hurting reliability” does. Then check whether that result would matter as much as you think. Halving an expense that barely costs anything isn't a snitch. A useful place to look is at something important that keeps failing to happen. A customer likes the product but won't expand. They have a long list of feature requests, so you keep building features. But perhaps they need a second department using the product before they can approve a bigger contract. Finishing the first department's list won't get you there. Learning that changes what you should do tomorrow. It may also make the work you've already done worth much more. Talk to the people who depend on the result. Find out what is actually stopping them. Before spending six months on your explanation, see whether you can test it in a week. And don't assume the snitch will be glamorous. It might be getting a deployment to work, fixing one persistent source of customer churn, or having a conversation you've been avoiding. What makes it the snitch is what happens when you catch it. V. Winning You can win on goals. An AE who makes quota through twenty small deals has made quota. Someone who does the ordinary work exceptionally well, month after month, can contribute an enormous amount. But you have to know whether the goals you're scoring are enough. You can be ahead for most of a Quidditch match and still lose when the other team catches the snitch. Being busy all afternoon doesn't change the final score. The same problem shows up in a company that keeps signing customers and keeps losing them. Sales may be doing everything right. Everyone may be working hard. But if customers leave faster than you can replace them, doing more of the same won't be enough. Someone has to go after the reason they leave. You can lose by never looking for the thing that would decide the game. You can also lose by doing nothing else. Some people spend months “working on strategy” without getting close to an actual result. My hire was working three accounts. He had customers to convince and deals to close. Calling yourself a seeker doesn't put points on the board. And even a catch isn't always enough. Krum catches the snitch in the World Cup final and Bulgaria still loses because they're too far behind (and yes, I said books. If you've only seen the movies reconsider your life choices). If pursuing one customer costs you the rest of your business, closing them doesn't make it a good trade. You should know your snitch even if you decide to keep scoring goals. You should have some idea of what would be worth dropping the next assignment for. Otherwise, it's easy to spend all your time on the work that arrives and never pursue the result that would make the biggest difference. I nearly fired someone for making that decision better than I had. I haven't assigned him a task in a long time. I still have plenty of things I'd like done. He's not going to do them. That's fine with me, because he's my seeker. Blandly,

post.author: Alex
post.text: Hi, I'm Alex, cofounder at @relate_studio. In this tutorial, I'll walk you through how we design brand mascots with AI: finding first concepts in Krea, refining the best direction in Nano Banana 2, generating new poses and angles, and turning everything into a concept you can scale. A lot of brand designers shy away from projects like this because mascot design feels like something that requires strong illustration or 3D skills. In reality, AI tools alone can already get you to a result strong enough to present to a client and detailed enough for a motion designer to use as reference for a full 3D build. For the sake of this article, I will show you how we made the following mascot for the Yoru project 1. Gather references and define the mascot Start by collecting references in Figma and deciding what kind of personality, proportions, materials, and overall style you want. For this mascot, we wanted a stylized 3D anthropomorphic character. Most of my references were 3D, but I also included a few 2D examples. One of them actually had more personality than any of the 3D references. Don't limit yourself to references that look exactly like the final result. Mixing different styles can lead to more interesting generations. 2. Generate rough concepts in Krea For early exploration, we used Krea. It's convenient because you can access multiple AI models from a single interface instead of constantly jumping between tools. Upload a few references and start generating rough concepts. At this stage, the goal isn't to get a perfect mascot. You're just looking for interesting shapes, proportions, clothes, expressions, and personalities worth developing further. Prompt: "3D stylized mascot character, anthropomorphic rabbit, cocky and playful attitude, standing pose, wearing dark bomber jacket, soft rubber/plastic material look, rounded friendly proportions, big expressive eyes, thick fluffy tail, clean isolated character on dark background, front three-quarter view, high detail, centered composition." Pro-tip: You can also let Krea generate the prompt for you by dragging a reference image into the prompt field. 3. Pick the strongest base Then, after multiple generations, select the best result. Don't worry about small mistakes yet! The version I picked had a strange artifact on the pant leg and inconsistent color on the jacket, but the overall anatomy and proportions were strong. At this stage, it's much more important to get the silhouette, personality, and proportions right than to polish every detail. 4. Refine the mascot in Nano Banana 2 Next, take the strongest concept into Nano Banana 2 and clean it up. You can fix textures, colors, clothing details, backgrounds, and unwanted artifacts with simple prompts. Prompt: "Remove the noise from the BG, make the BG white. Remove the pocket outline from the bomber jacket." Instead of trying to solve everything in one huge prompt, I usually make small changes one at a time. It's easier to control the result and understand what each prompt changed. 5. Generate new poses and angles Once the main character design is locked, you can start generating different poses. Find pose references you like and ask the model to reproduce them while keeping the mascot's appearance, anatomy, clothes, and proportions consistent. Prompt: "Create a new pose strictly using the appearance and anatomy of the mascot on the first image. Use the second image as a pose reference. Do not change the clothes of the mascot and his appearance." 6. Build the presentation The final step is to put the mascot into actual design compositions. For this project, I created three posters around the character. This helps prove that the mascot isn't just an isolated AI generation, but part of a visual system that can work across the brand. At this point, you already have a coherent concept you can put in front of a client. You don't necessarily need to build the final production-ready 3D model yourself. These generations can serve as a detailed visual reference for an illustrator, 3D artist, or motion designer who takes the mascot into production (which we often do at @relate_studio. 7. Scaling the approach Once the character is established, you can keep expanding it with new poses, expressions, compositions, environments, and campaign ideas. The important part is locking the character's core visual language first. From there, AI becomes a fast way to explore how the mascot can live across websites, social media, motion, advertising, and other brand materials. You don't need to be an illustrator or 3D designer to explore mascot concepts anymore. You mainly need a strong visual direction, good references, and the ability to judge which outputs are actually worth developing. However, for concepts that you'd like to scale, like we did with Jupiter, it can be helpful to handcraft the mascot after you achieve a great concept About Us @relate_studio is an international, full-cycle design studio. Our portfolio includes Jupiter, Sui, Solana, fomo, Mysten Labs, Crypto.com, and hundreds of other companies. We use AI regularly, but not as a replacement for design thinking. We use it where it saves time without sacrificing quality. If you need help with design, schedule a call at relate.studio.

post.author: Rohan Nayak
post.text: We grew from ~0 to $500M ARR, adding $250M last year alone while being EBITDA profitable. 1,300-word post on every growth tactic that worked for us: 1. What got us from 0-$400M ARR in the US works in every country. 2. Retention and Monetisation Hacks. 3. Localization > Translation. 4. Experiment with $1M internal seed checks. 5. Pivoting to only AI content production unlocked 100% ARR growth. Pocket FM is like Netflix for audio-only dramas, with our own pool of one-person studios. 1. Acquisition Playbook for 0-$10M ARR in any country in 6 months We run a 90 sec video trailer of an audio drama as an Ad and ask users to download the app if they're interested in the rest of the story. Our core insight after spending >$100M on acquisition is: If the clickthrough rate (CTR) for an ad goes from 2% to 2.25%, our customer acquisition cost (CAC) decreases by ~ 30%. We remodelled our system around this insight and built an AI-first 2.25% CTR ad manufacturing machine that works in every country. For every new country, we take our hit shows -> use LLMs to extract and most intriguing moments -> Write a 5-min script combining all the best parts. The first 60 seconds has to have a hook every 5 seconds and needs to end with a crazy cliffhanger to force a download mid-scroll. If a marketing video is not hitting our benchmarks (2.5% CTR and 55% 3-second through-play), a creative director gets involved to change the hook or cliffhanger to get the numbers there. AI lets us make 1,000 Ads per show, and in total we do ~17.5k Ads per month. When a business creating scales from 1k to 10k Ads, the normal thing is for CAC to skyrocket. But with what I just shared, we 7-8x'd our User Acquisition budget without increasing our CAC materially. It took us 8 months to figure this out, but then the timeline from 0-$10M in every country got shorter and shorter: US revenue grew to $25M in 19 months. (US is now 78% of total) Germany to 21M in 11 months. France to $10M in 3 months. 2. Retention and Monetisation Hacks. We knew we wanted to create an audio entertainment platform, but there was no standard format. For the first 2-3 years, we tried 10 different formats before landing on the winner. After we got it right with audio drama (8-12min chapters, written for mobile fiction, serialized, episodes have strong hooks and end on cliffhangers), avg daily streaming time went from ~25mins to 150+. Audio drama made us realize that Pocket FM was creating a whole new medium. There was no playbook for anything that we were doing. Everything had to be thought & built from scratch. This is what we did for each major bullet: - Monetization: Users have some free daily minutes to listen; then it's pay per episode. We also added the option for users to unlock episodes by watching ads, which is doing extremely well. Ads scaled from zero to a ~$90M run rate in 12 months. - Engagement & production: You don't become obsessed with an app you open once a week. To have users engage daily, we make the next episode free every day. Also helps them build the habit. - Discovery. Huge problem because people consuming Pocket FM enter the app, tap the show, and lock the screen. We fixed it by doing "playlists" of episodes. Once users's free minutes on a show are done, we ask users if they want to pay. If they say no, we play a new show, one where they haven't used their free mins. And we stitch episodes of different shows together that way, creating natural discovery. 3. Localization > translation. 78% of our revenue is still concentrated in the US. Localisation is fixing this: You might write a show for a Spanish audience where language, jokes, folklore, have a certain flavor; if you merely translate the show for, say, a Norwegian audience, that color is lost and hurts the show in the Norway. Listeners would relate more if the show was written by a Norwegian. That's why, instead of translating, we localize shows to different regions. We use AI to take the spine of stories and adapt their whole cultural layer to the other country. The results: a US show that was localized for a German audience had 50% higher retention than the translated version. Localization + our user acquisition playbook led to: - $10M+ ARR in France within 3 months - $21M+ ARR in Germany within 11 months. And this expands writers' addressable market. We get messages of writers thrilled to have revenue coming from the US, India, EU, LatAm, without them doing much incremental work. 4. Experiment. We give $1M checks to new internal initiatives, and the team has 12-18 months to prove their thesis. If they prove it, we double down. This is how Pocket Saga came about, our AI video microdrama app. It's an AI video equivalent of Pocket FM. Same shows and structure, but as a vertical 2-min mobile video series. We launched it two months ago and it's at ~$15M ARR. Pocket's broader thesis is to help creators tell their stories to as many people as possible. Start with audio drama -> multiple languages or localize to diff countries -> microdrama -> more formats like movies, TV shows, and games. Best of all is that writers get revenue streams not only from countries they wouldn't have tapped into, but also from formats they wouldn't have thought possible. 5. Pivoting to only AI content production unlocked 100% ARR growth. In mid-2024, we pivoted to only AI content production. Our growth took a very direct hit. Pocket was already at $200M ARR, growing 50% YoY, and we flatlined for a whole semester. Six months later, the business exploded. After the switch, we went from ~25k hours of content produced per year to over 2.5M hours, which are also higher quality.
